q.intro.text: A line, and two slope triangles on it. Jo's small triangle goes three across and two up: a slope of two thirds.

q.ask.text: Kai draws a bigger triangle on the same line: six across, four up. What slope does Kai's triangle show? Pick one, and say how sure you are.

e.intro.text: Four steps. Press each one: the picture moves first, then the notation.

e.s0.text: Jo's triangle: three across, the run, and two up, the rise. Slope is rise divided by run: two thirds. The line climbs two thirds for every one across.

e.s1.text: The bottom legs are both horizontal, so they are parallel. The line crosses them at the same angle, corresponding angles, and both triangles have a right angle. Two equal angles: the triangles are similar.

e.s2.text: Similar triangles keep their sides in the same ratio. Kai's: four up for six across, and four sixths is two thirds. The same slope, anywhere on the line.

e.s3.text: Take any point x, y on the line. Its triangle from the point where the line meets the y axis has run x and rise y minus one, and its slope is two thirds too. So y minus one is two thirds x, and y equals two thirds x plus one.

e.why.text: Quick check: why does Kai's big triangle give the same slope as Jo's small one?

e.why.ok.text: Yes. Same angles, so the sides keep the same ratio: rise divided by run stays two thirds.

e.why.look.text: They do look alike, but looks can fool you. The reason is the equal angles: the corresponding angles at the parallel legs, and the right angles.

e.why.size.text: Then a bigger triangle would show a bigger slope, and it doesn't: four sixths is two thirds. Size does not change the ratio.

t.intro.text: A candle is six inches tall and burns down at a steady rate. The graph shows its height for twelve hours. The first step is done for you.

t.s0.text: From the start to the point two, five: run two, rise negative one. The slope is negative one half.

t.rise.text: Now a big triangle on the same line, from two, five to eight, two. Its run is six. What is its rise? Use a minus sign if it goes down.

t.rise.ok.text: Yes: down three, so the rise is negative three.

t.rise.sign.text: The candle gets shorter: the height goes down three. A drop is a negative rise: negative three.

t.rise.no.text: Count the squares from a height of five down to two.

t.slope.text: So what slope does the big triangle show?

t.slope.ok.text: Yes: negative three divided by six is negative one half, the same as the small triangle. The candle loses half an inch each hour.

t.slope.sign.text: The height goes down, so the slope is negative: negative one half.

t.slope.inv.text: That is run divided by rise. Slope is rise divided by run: negative three divided by six.

t.slope.rise.text: Negative three is the rise for six hours. Divide it by the run, six.

t.eq.text: Last step: which equation is the candle's line? Start with its height at zero hours.

t.eq.ok.text: Yes: it starts at six inches and changes by negative one half inch each hour.

t.eq.swap.text: The number times x is the slope, negative one half. The number added is the start, six.

t.eq.drop.text: That line goes through the origin, but the candle starts at six inches.

t.eq.sign.text: A slope of positive one half would make the candle grow. It burns down: negative one half.

t.cb.right.text: At the start you picked two thirds for Kai, and you were right. Now you can say why: similar triangles keep rise divided by run the same.

t.cb.double.text: At the start you picked four thirds: twice the triangle, twice the slope. But the run doubled too, so the ratio stayed two thirds.

t.cb.rise.text: At the start you picked four, the rise on its own. Slope divides the rise by the run: four divided by six is two thirds.

t.cb.none.text: On a straight line, every slope triangle gives the same rise divided by run.

t.cb.sure.text: And you were certain, so this one is worth remembering.

p.intro.text: Riley says: the line y equals two x plus three has the same slope everywhere. So y over x is the same at every point too, and the line is proportional. Is Riley right?

p.test.text: Let's test it. Build the argument and see where it leads.

p.build.text: Now prove it. Fill each because with the reason that makes the line true.

p.c1.text: Right. Two slope triangles, and both go up two for each one across.

p.c2.text: Right. The dashed lines from the origin through the two points have different slopes: y over x is five, then three.

p.c3.text: Right. The line crosses the y axis at three, not at zero. Riley's claim is false.

p.no.prop.text: Every straight line is linear, but proportional needs more: it must go through the origin.

p.no.ratio.text: That is exactly Riley's slip. Check y over x at two points: five and three.

p.no.other.text: True, but it is the reason for a different line. Which reason makes this line true?

p.done.text: That's a proof: three claims, each with its reason, and the picture backs every one. A constant slope gives a constant y over x only when b is zero.
